performers: Carl Martin Öhmann, tenor; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Kerstin Thorborg sings the alto songs of the same concert)
intro: Friends drink, talk and write verses in a green-and-white porcelain pavilion. Mahler paints this small scene with bright woodwinds, then turns it upside down in the pond.

sections.label: A · A porcelain pavilion
sections.mNote: Woodwind trills and bouncing strings surround the tenor

sections.label: B · Friends drinking and writing verses
sections.mNote: G major brings chattering clarinets and a muted trumpet

sections.label: C · The pavilion in the pond

cues.title: A pavilion made of woodwinds
cues.text: A horn note and a touch of triangle open this tiny scene. Flutes, oboe and clarinets trade trills and quick, neat figures. When the tenor describes the porcelain pavilion, violins and violas join him with a bouncing bow-stroke.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition full score, pp. 51–52, opening and rehearsal figure 2: winds, horn and triangle, followed by tenor and saltando strings. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sleeves rolled up for verses
cues.text: The music turns to G major, with chattering clarinets and a muted trumpet. Inside the little pavilion, friends drink, talk and write verses. Their silk sleeves are pushed back; their caps sit low on their necks.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 53–56, figures 5–9: G-major signature, muted trumpet and the friends’ scene. German text and its earlier versions: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Jugend.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pavilion that never stood
cues.text: The porcelain pavilion began as a mistranslation. Li Bai’s poem is called “Banquet at Tao’s Family Pavilion”, and the Chinese word for the surname Tao can also mean porcelain. Judith Gautier’s French turned the family’s house into china; Bethge and Mahler kept it.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Von der Jugend page, gives Li Bai’s “Banquet at Tao’s Family Pavilion”, Gautier’s mistranslation of the double-meaning character and her French “Le pavillon de porcelaine”, with Bethge’s and Mahler’s texts: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Jugend.htm

cues.title: The pond becomes a mirror
cues.text: A solo violin sings above rocking strings as the music slows into G minor. The tenor describes the pond’s still surface. Everything the song has shown us is there again, reflected in the water.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 57–58, figure 10, Ruhiger: solo violin, rocking strings and the tenor’s words about the reflection.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Toblach, summer 1908
cues.text: Mahler composes the songs largely in the summer of 1908, forbidden the long walks he needs. From Bethge’s 83 paraphrases of 38 poets he chooses seven. In early September he reports to Bruno Walter: “I was very diligent … I believe it is the most personal thing I have yet created.”
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s introduction for Universal Edition, March 2010, gives the doctors’ restrictions, the 83 paraphrases of 38 poets, the seven chosen and Mahler’s letter to Walter of early September 1908: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: The bridge turns upside down
cues.text: The first tempo returns suddenly in B♭ major, and the strings take off their mutes. In the tenor’s words, everything stands on its head: pavilion, friends and the bridge, whose reflected arch becomes a half-moon.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 59–60, figure 14: Tempo I subito, Dämpfer ab and the reordered final stanzas. Mahler Archives prints Mahler’s text beside Bethge’s.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A muted trumpet in G major
transitions.to: B · Friends drinking and writing verses
transitions.how: Oboes and clarinets carry the quick figures out of B♭ major. At rehearsal figure 5 the signature changes to G major: a muted trumpet joins the woodwinds, clarinets repeat little chords and the triangle keeps shimmering. The tenor enters a few bars later with the friends in the pavilion.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition full score, pp. 52–54, figures 5–6.

transitions.title: A solo violin darkens the pond
transitions.from: B · Friends drinking and writing verses
transitions.to: C · The pavilion in the pond
transitions.how: The woodwind figures subside while a solo violin carries a longer line. At Ruhiger, G turns from major to minor. The strings rock quietly beneath the violin, and the tenor begins to describe the scene’s reflection.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 57, figure 10: Ruhiger, solo violin and the change to G minor.

transitions.title: The mutes come off
transitions.from: C · The pavilion in the pond
transitions.to: A′ · Everything standing on its head
transitions.how: Repeated ritardandos slow the strings almost to a halt. Tempo I subito brings the opening pace back at once, with flutes and oboes in B♭ major. The strings remove their mutes and resume their bouncing accompaniment as the tenor describes the world standing on its head.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 58–59, figures 11–14, successive slowing and Tempo I subito.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, III. Von der Jugend, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 51–60: woodwind opening; strings and tenor at figure 2; G major at figure 5; Ruhiger at figure 10; Tempo I subito at figure 14.

timeline.note: A held horn note and soft triangle strokes open the song.
Second flute and oboe weave a quick figure over the horn.
Piccolo, flutes and clarinets trade trills above the horn’s repeated notes.
The tenor enters with bouncing bow-strokes in violins and violas.
G major brings chattering clarinets, a muted trumpet and triangle.
Violins and violas bow near the fingerboard beneath the friends’ conversation.
A solo violin rises above the tenor and the other strings.
At Ruhiger, rocking strings support the solo violin and tenor.
The tenor’s reflection scene slows over held winds and plucked basses.
Flutes and oboes restore the first tempo; unmuted strings accompany the tenor.
Woodwinds and upper strings hold the final pianississimo chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Kerstin Thorborg does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
